issue.issue_text: Whether the condition requiring an assurance from an Embassy/High Commission for bail is practical and whether the issue needs to be referred to a larger Bench for reconsideration.

facts: An appellant, a Nigerian national, was granted bail with several conditions.

One of the conditions required the appellant to obtain a 'certificate of assurance' from the High Commission of Nigeria, stating that the accused would not leave the country and would appear in court when required.
The appellant challenged this condition, arguing it was impractical and impossible to fulfill.
law: The Court considered a previous ruling (Clause (iv)) that directed Special Judges to insist on such a certificate from the embassy of a foreign-accused.
The Court also relied on the fundamental legal principle that a condition for bail cannot be impossible for the accused to comply with, as such a condition would effectively deny bail.
application: The Court first acknowledged that it was unlikely that any embassy or high commission would be able to provide such an assurance, making the condition inherently impractical.

It reasoned that the issuance of such a certificate is entirely beyond the control of the accused. If an embassy refuses or fails to issue the certificate in a reasonable time (suggested as seven days), the accused, who is otherwise entitled to bail, would be unfairly denied their liberty.
The Court determined that this condition is not mandatory in every case involving a foreign national. Its imposition should depend on the specific facts and circumstances of the case.

It held that even if such a condition is imposed, the court retains the power to dispense with or delete it if it cannot be met. In such a scenario, the court can impose alternative, more practical conditions like surrendering the passport and requiring regular reporting to the police or court.
By clarifying that the condition is not absolute and can be waived, the Court found it was not necessary to refer the issue to a larger bench for reconsideration.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it was not necessary to refer the issue to a larger bench. It held that the condition requiring a certificate of assurance from an embassy is not mandatory in every case and that courts have the power to waive or delete this condition if it proves impossible for the accused to fulfill. Accordingly, the Court ordered the condition to be deleted from the appellant's bail order.

issue.issue_text: Whether a bail condition requiring an assurance from an Embassy/High Commission offends the rights of the accused under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.

facts: An accused foreign national was granted bail in a case under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985.
The bail order included a condition requiring the accused to obtain a 'certificate of assurance' from their Embassy/High Commission.
This certificate was meant to assure the court that the accused would not leave the country and would appear for trial when required.
The accused challenged this condition, arguing it was onerous and violated their rights.
law: Under Article 21 of the Constitution of India, every person, including a foreign national, has a right to life and personal liberty.
An accused person is presumed innocent until proven guilty and cannot be deprived of all their rights under Article 21.
Bail conditions cannot be so onerous or impossible to comply with that they effectively frustrate the order of bail itself.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that obtaining a certificate from an Embassy or High Commission is a matter entirely beyond the control of the accused.
An accused person has no power to compel their country's embassy to issue such a certificate.
If the embassy declines or fails to issue the certificate within a reasonable time (the court suggested seven days), the accused would be unable to meet the bail condition.
This would result in the accused remaining in custody despite being held entitled to bail, effectively denying them their liberty due to an impossible condition.
The Court determined that denying bail on the ground of non-compliance with a condition that is impossible for the accused to fulfill is unjust and infringes on their rights under Article 21.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that requiring a certificate of assurance from an embassy is not a mandatory condition for granting bail to a foreign national. The Court held that if such a condition is imposed and cannot be met within a reasonable time, the court has the power to dispense with or delete it. The Court stated that denying bail for failure to comply with an impossible condition offends the accused's rights under Article 21. Instead, other conditions like surrendering the passport and regularly reporting to the police can be imposed. In the specific case, the Court ordered the condition to be deleted.

issue.issue_text: What is the scope of the phrase "interest of justice" under Section 437(3)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for imposing bail conditions?

law.name: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC), Section 437(3)
law.summary: This section empowers a court to impose conditions when granting bail. Clause (c) specifically allows for any other condition the court considers necessary "in the interest of justice."

law.name: Kunal Kumar Tiwari v. State of Bihar
law.summary: A Supreme Court precedent which held that the phrase "interest of justice" in Section 437(3)(c) means "good administration of justice" or "advancing the trial process," and that a broader meaning should be avoided.

law.name: Constitution of India, Article 21
law.summary: Guarantees the right to life and personal liberty. The Court noted that even an accused person retains rights under this article, which can only be curtailed to the minimum extent necessary.

application.description: The Supreme Court began by affirming that the phrase "interest of justice" in Section 437(3)(c) of the CrPC cannot be given a broad or expansive meaning.

Relying on its previous decision in *Kunal Kumar Tiwari v. State of Bihar*, the Court defined the scope of "interest of justice" narrowly, stating it means "good administration of justice" or "advancing the trial process."
The Court established that any conditions imposed under this clause must not be "fanciful, arbitrary or freakish." They must be consistent with the specific objectives of bail.

It outlined the legitimate objectives for imposing bail conditions: to ensure the accused does not obstruct the investigation, remains available for trial, does not tamper with evidence, does not commit other offenses, and does not hinder the conclusion of the trial.
The Court emphasized that while imposing conditions, the constitutional rights of the accused under Article 21 can only be curtailed to the minimum extent required to achieve these objectives.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the scope of the phrase "interest of justice" under Section 437(3)(c) of the CrPC is narrow and purposive. It does not grant courts the power to impose arbitrary or fanciful conditions. Any condition must be directly aimed at ensuring the proper administration of justice and the smooth progression of the trial, while minimally infringing upon the accused's constitutional rights.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: While imposing bail conditions under Section 437(3)(c), the phrase 'interest of justice' must be interpreted purposively to mean 'good administration of justice' or 'advancing the trial process'; any conditions imposed cannot be arbitrary, fanciful, or extend beyond this purpose.
obiter: Prima facie, we are of the view that none of the Embassies/High Commissions may be able to give assurances as mentioned in Clause (iv). The question is whether we need to refer this case to a larger Bench for re-consideration of Clause (iv).

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The phrase “interest of justice” under Section 437(3)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure must be interpreted narrowly to mean “good administration of justice” or “advancing the trial process.” A broader meaning cannot be assigned, and any conditions imposed under this clause cannot be arbitrary, fanciful, or freakish. The purpose of such conditions is strictly to ensure the accused does not interfere with the investigation, remains available for trial, does not tamper with evidence, and does not obstruct the expeditious conclusion of the trial.
legal_tests_applied: Purposive Interpretation: The court applied a purposive interpretation to the phrase “interest of justice,” holding that its meaning must be confined to the object of the provision, which is to advance the trial process.
Arbitrariness Test: Bail conditions cannot be “arbitrary, fanciful or freakish” and must be consistent with the object of imposing conditions.

Minimum Curtailment Test: When imposing bail conditions, the Constitutional rights of an accused under Article 21 can be curtailed only to the minimum extent required to achieve the objectives of bail.
